work.s1Desc: The scanner reads the page and scripts that a normal visitor can download. It does not log in or test private addresses.

faq.subtitle: The public scan and the deeper review answer different questions.
faq.q1: My app works. Why does it still need <brand></brand>?
faq.a1: A working screen does not prove that data, paid actions, or administrative routes are protected. The scan looks for evidence a normal browser can reach.
faq.q2: What does the public scan check?
faq.a2: It checks public pages and scripts for exposed secret-looking values, risky configuration, and missing browser security headers. It cannot prove that private database rules are correct.
faq.q3: Does the scan need source code or a database password?
faq.a3: No. The public scan reads only the address you submit and the files available to a normal visitor. A deeper review uses only access agreed in advance.
faq.q4: Can a repair change application behaviour?
faq.a4: Yes. Closing an open data path or moving a decision to the server can expose an existing dependency. Changes should be tested before release.
faq.q5: Does every application need a rebuild?
faq.a5: No. Many issues can be repaired in the existing application. A rebuild is considered only when the evidence shows that a safe repair would cost more or leave important risks.
faq.a6: Scope and price depend on the application, the access available, and the checks required. aiNOW confirms those details before any paid work starts.
faq.q7: What if the public scan finds nothing?
faq.a7: That means no listed issue was detected in the public files. It does not confirm sign-in rules, database permissions, payments, or private services.
faq.q8: How long does a deeper review take?
faq.a8: Timing is set after the application and access scope are understood. The plan separates review time from repair time.
faq.q9: Can my developer implement the repairs?
faq.a9: Yes. The report is written around evidence, affected areas, repair steps, and verification so your chosen developer can use it.
faq.q10: Do I have to leave my AI coding platform?
faq.a10: Not automatically. The review identifies which risks can be fixed in the current setup and where stronger source control, testing, or release controls are needed.
faq.q11: Can an AI coding tool still be used afterwards?
faq.a11: Yes. Sensitive decisions should be protected by server checks and tests so later edits cannot silently reopen the same path.
faq.q12: How is access handled for a deeper review?
faq.a12: Access, confidentiality, test data, and removal of access are agreed before the review. Production passwords are not a default requirement.
faq.q13: Can the report support technical due diligence?
faq.a13: It can document what was checked, what evidence was found, what was repaired, and which items remain. The recipient decides whether that scope meets the diligence need.
faq.q14: What should I do if a live secret is exposed?
faq.a14: Revoke or rotate the exposed value, remove it from public files, move sensitive work to the server, and rescan before relying on the repair.

ten.heading: Ten places an AI-built app can expose business risk.
ten.subtitle: Each item names a check, not a claim about your application. Open a row to see the risk and the reference behind it.
ten.b1: A public project key may identify the database. Row-level rules decide which records each request may read or change.
ten.t2: A secret is shipped to the browser
ten.b2: Any value sent in a page or script can be read by a visitor. Sensitive keys belong in a protected server environment.
ten.t3: Sign-in does not prove identity correctly
ten.b3: Weak session, recovery, or account checks can let one user act as another. Authentication needs explicit tests.
ten.t4: Paid access is decided on the client
ten.b4: A browser value can be changed locally. The server must authorise the paid action before returning the result.
ten.b5: File type, storage access, size, and download permissions need separate controls. A hidden link is not access control.
ten.t6: Production data has no safe recovery path
ten.b6: Backups, restore tests, and separation between test and production data limit the effect of an accidental destructive action.
ten.b7: Access control, injection, unsafe design, configuration, and outdated components need scenario-based checks before release.
ten.b8: An expensive endpoint needs request limits, budget controls, and monitoring so one account cannot consume unlimited resources.
ten.s8: OWASP API Security Top 10: Unrestricted Resource Consumption
ten.t9: The same business rule is copied across files
ten.b9: Duplicated security decisions drift apart. One protected path may be fixed while another copy remains open.
ten.t10: The application cannot be handed over safely
ten.b10: Source history, tests, release steps, and access ownership let another responsible developer verify and maintain the application.
ten.note: The checklist avoids market-size claims and customer statistics. The result for your application must come from its own evidence.

fix.heading: Finding a key is only the first step.
fix.subtitle: A complete repair revokes the old value, moves the replacement to the server, and checks the public files again.
fix.redacted: The sample value is masked and cannot be used.
fix.scanningText: Checking the public files available to a browser.
fix.exposedText: A masked key-like value appears in a public file.
fix.revokingText: Revoking the old value so it can no longer authorise requests.
fix.serverSideText: The replacement moves to the server and is no longer sent to the browser.
fix.rescanningText: Checking the same public files again.
fix.cleanText: The rescan finds no key in the browser files.
fix.outcome: The old value is revoked, the replacement stays on the server, and the public rescan is clean.
